item.title: iPhone Duo launches Friday — order limits, first unboxing, and Samsung's foldable counterattack
item.description:
The iPhone Duo goes on sale this Friday, October 23, and the week leading up to launch is unfolding like a case study in supply-constrained demand. The first unboxing video from outside the press has surfaced, showing the device ships flat rather than folded and is otherwise packaged like any other iPhone. Reviews are expected tomorrow, and leaked App Store screenshots of Apple's built-in apps on the Duo show iPad-like landscape interfaces with sidebar navigation — a first real look at day-to-day use.

Demand is clearly straining supply: Apple is limiting orders to two per customer in the US, UK, and elsewhere after shipping dates slipped into January within minutes of pre-orders opening, an explicit move against scalpers. And Samsung is reportedly spooked, with plans to launch six different foldable phones next year in an attempt to counter the Duo — even before Apple's device has shipped a single unit to a customer.

Sources

  • MacRumors: First iPhone Duo Unboxing Video Appears Ahead of Friday Launch
  • MacRumors: Here's What Apple's Apps Look Like on the iPhone Duo
  • 9to5Mac: iPhone Duo orders limited to two per customer as Apple tackles scalping
  • 9to5Mac: Samsung fighting iPhone Duo by launching six foldable phones next year

item.title: Apple deepens US manufacturing push with titanium, camera deals and Houston Mac mini assembly
item.description:
Apple is making its most aggressive case yet for domestic manufacturing. The company announced new and expanded American Manufacturing Program partnerships: up to $100 million over three years to Pennsylvania-based Perryman, which produces the titanium used in iPhone Duo enclosures, and an extended deal with Delaware-based Qnity Electronics to make advanced films for the variable aperture camera on the iPhone 18 Pro. All told, Apple says nearly 100 components across the two phones are produced by American companies in more than a dozen states.

Apple reiterated that Mac mini assembly in the US will begin later this year, with Foxconn building the computers in Houston, Texas; US-assembled units will primarily serve the US market. The announcements fit Apple's broader pledge to invest in domestic manufacturing.

item.title: Taction wants more money after record $5.7 billion patent verdict against Apple
item.description:
The record-breaking $5.7 billion jury verdict against Apple may not be the end of the story. Taction Technology is asking a federal judge to award hundreds of millions more, arguing the September verdict only covers sales from 2021 through late March 2026 — and that Apple also owes prejudgment interest plus royalties on future sales.

The jury found that Apple's Taptic Engine infringed two Taction patents covering haptic feedback — the taps and vibrations in devices — though the infringement was not found to be willful. Apple disputes the verdict entirely and is seeking to have it overturned or to get a new trial. If the award stands, it would be among the largest patent verdicts in history, and ongoing royalties would turn a one-time penalty into a continuing cost on every iPhone and Apple Watch sold.

Sources

  • MacRumors: Apple Could Owe Even More After $5.7 Billion Patent Verdict
  • AppleInsider: Taction won record-breaking $5.7 billion verdict against Apple, asks for more

item.title: iPad mini 8 with OLED and touchscreen MacBook Pro expected at next week's event
item.description:
Apple's October 28 experience in Los Angeles is shaping up to be a hardware-heavy event. The headliner is expected to be the iPad mini 8 with an OLED display, powered by the A20 Pro chip built on TSMC's 2nm process — promising roughly 1.5× faster CPU and 2.5× faster GPU performance over the A17 Pro. Hands-on time at the event is reportedly being arranged for invitees.

Also expected: a redesigned MacBook Pro with a touch-enabled OLED display — several firsts for the Mac — alongside a 14-inch MacBook Pro with the M6 chip and an M6 iMac. Rumors point to a lighter, possibly thinner chassis that ditches the notch.

Sources

  • MacRumors: Apple's Touchscreen OLED MacBook Pro: Everything We Know

item.title: Perplexity's AI agent now runs entirely on your Mac — with a 36GB RAM caveat
item.description:
Perplexity announced a local-first mode for Computer that lets its AI agent work entirely on your Mac — model, task planning, reasoning, and file processing all handled on-device, even without an internet connection — sending data to the cloud only with the user's approval. It runs on Qwen 3.6 or Perplexity's post-trained PPLX Pro in the Perplexity app for Mac on supported Apple silicon machines, with code and tool execution isolated in sandboxes, and it can operate native Mac apps. The local mode, available to Pro, Max, and Enterprise subscribers, complements September's Hybrid Compute update.

Sources

item.title: HomeView was ready for years — it just had to wait for Siri AI
item.description:
Apple's $299 HomeView home hub was reportedly mostly finished for years, kept in limbo while the company waited on Siri AI. Now that both are out, Apple executives are framing the delay as necessary: the new Siri AI is the "magic" of HomeView, in the words of VP of product marketing Kaiann Drance, but its power is in how little users have to interact with it.

The killer features, Apple says, are simplicity and an assistant good enough to stay in the background — the device "comes together in a way that we haven't been able to deliver before," per Drance. It's a revealing explanation for the long-rumored device's endless delays, and a bet that an AI assistant, not another screen, is the missing piece of the smart-home hub.

Sources

  • AppleInsider: Simplicity and Siri AI are the HomeView's killer features, says Apple
  • 9to5Mac: Apple explains why HomeView couldn’t launch until now

item.title: iOS 27 adds scam protection; iOS 27.2 and tvOS 27.2 arrive next week
item.description:
Apple's software week is packed. iOS 27 introduces "Impersonation Risk Detection," a new security feature that protects against scams — but it's off by default, so users will need to enable it manually. Next week brings iOS 27.2 with new features across six Apple apps, plus tvOS 27.2 with three new features for Apple TV 4K owners, including screen saver upgrades.

On the hardware side, the new fourth-generation Apple TV 4K can connect to up to four HomePods in front-left, front-right, rear-left, and rear-right positions for an all-Apple surround sound system — and a quieter new feature, Whole Room Audio, spreads sound evenly across the four speakers for parties or game day. Separately, Australian carrier Telstra briefly posted (then deleted) a support document saying RCS support would arrive in a December iOS update, pointing to iOS 27.3.

Sources

item.title: UK regulator says Apple's NFC opening still doesn't let Apple Pay rivals compete
item.description:
The UK's Competition and Markets Authority says Apple's concessions on iPhone NFC access still don't make it practical for developers to build genuine Apple Pay competitors. Despite Apple loosening its grip on the NFC chip under EU pressure, the CMA says developers report that high fees, strict terms, and technical restrictions are holding up wider third-party adoption — the same complaints that followed Apple's 2024 investigation into digital wallets and its European agreement.

The UK is now pushing for easier access at no cost for its own developers, arguing that simply mirroring the EU's terms won't cut it. It's the latest sign that regulators are treating Apple's payment chip as infrastructure that should be open — and that the compromises Apple struck in Europe are becoming a floor, not a ceiling, for what watchdogs demand elsewhere.

Sources

  • AppleInsider: EU iPhone NFC concessions don't go far enough, says UK
  • 9to5Mac: Apple still makes it too hard for Apple Pay competitors to emerge, says UK

item.title: Apple Sets October 28 'Pro and Tell' Event
item.description:
Apple is not done with 2026 yet. Greg Joswiak posted "Can't wait to pro and tell next week" on X, confirming a media experience in Los Angeles on Wednesday, October 28 at 10:00 a.m. Pacific, with everyone else getting the announcements via press releases. It's the second unconventional event of the month, following the October 13 "Welcome Home" announcement of HomeView, the new Apple TV 4K, and HomePod mini 2.

The headliner is expected to be the long-rumored touchscreen MacBook Pro with an OLED display — and the "Pro" in the tagline strongly suggests Apple will stick with MacBook Pro branding rather than the once-rumored "MacBook Ultra" name, just as the "iPhone Ultra" ended up shipping as iPhone Duo. Also rumored: an M6 entry-level MacBook Pro, an M6 iMac, and an iPad mini with an OLED display. After surprise Mac launches in August and the September iPhone event, this is shaping up to be one of Apple's busiest falls ever.

item.title: iPhone Duo Launch: Capped Orders, No Walk-Ins, Shifting Delivery Dates
item.description:
The iPhone Duo launches Friday, October 23, and getting one will not be easy. Apple is limiting U.S. customers to two Duos per order, and in Japan and South Korea the Duo and iPhone 18 Pro Max will be reservation-only pickups — no walk-ins at launch, a mix of supply constraints and Apple's usual anti-scalping posture in Asia. Apple told outlets pre-order demand was "extraordinary," with stock selling out in moments amid manufacturing issues, so Apple Stores are expected to have little or no inventory on day one.

There is some relief: customers whose orders initially showed January delivery dates are seeing them bumped up, with some U.S. and Japanese pre-orders moving into a November 20–30 window. And one mystery is settled: an EU regulatory filing pegs the Duo's dual-battery capacity at 4,883 mAh, between the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max — though real-world tests already showed battery life on par with the 18 Pro.

item.title: Apple Acquires AI Audio Startup Samplab
item.description:
Apple quietly acquired Samplab, a Zurich-based AI audio editing company, back in June — revealed only now through a European Commission acquisitions filing. The deal covers certain assets and hires of Samplab employees, echoing Apple's similar arrangement with podcast AI firm Huxe. Samplab's tools convert audio to MIDI, detect and edit chords, split songs into stems, and edit individual notes within polyphonic audio without altering the original timbre.

The likely destination is Logic Pro and GarageBand. Logic already has Stem Splitter and Chord ID, but polyphonic note editing would be genuinely new — a meaningful creative upgrade for musicians working inside Apple's pro audio tools. Expect the technology to surface gradually in future Logic Pro releases rather than as a standalone announcement.

Sources

  • MacRumors: Apple Buys AI Audio Editing App Samplab

item.title: Release Candidates Land for iOS 27.2, macOS 27.2, and Nearly Everything Else
item.description:
Apple seeded the first release candidates of iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, macOS 27.2 Golden Gate, watchOS 27.2, tvOS 27.2, visionOS 27.2, and HomePod Software 27.2 to developers and public beta testers after four beta cycles, pointing to a public launch toward the end of October. The headline addition is Siri AI expanding to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish, alongside Siri AI support coming to Apple TV; macOS also gains new brightness and volume sliders.

Separately, Apple pushed third release candidates for the legacy branches — macOS Sequoia 15.8.2 and Tahoe 26.7.2 — continuing security and stability maintenance for machines not yet on Golden Gate. For users on older Macs, those updates remain the recommended path.

item.title: HomePod 27.2 Brings Sound Glow to Older Speakers and True Surround Sound
item.description:
HomePod Software 27.2 is quietly one of the more interesting point releases. Sound Glow — the feature that lights up the speaker's touch surface with colors pulsing to the album artwork, debuting on the HomePod mini 2 — is coming to the second-generation HomePod and the original HomePod mini as well.

Bigger still, tvOS 27.2 lays the groundwork for genuine home-theater surround sound: the new Apple TV 4K can drive four matched speakers (four HomePod mini 2s, four second-gen HomePods, or a mixed pair-plus-pair setup), configured right from the Apple TV with an option to kick off setup via the Remote app on iPhone. And for the annoyed: iOS 27.2 finally adds a setting to disable the touch controls on top of the HomePod entirely.

item.title: Apple's New App Store Chief Talks Gaming — Skeptics Unmoved
item.description:
Carson Oliver, Apple's new head of App Store Worldwide, gave an interview to Polygon laying out Apple's gaming ambitions: more premium iPhone titles, a growing pipeline of serious games, and a defined role for Apple Arcade. It is the clearest statement yet of how Apple sees the iPhone — and its ecosystem — as a gaming platform.

Not everyone is buying it. AppleInsider argues that despite the hardware being a gaming powerhouse, Apple still doesn't understand what gamers actually want from a mobile platform, pointing to a history of executives declaring Apple "serious about gaming" without following through beyond financial success. The interview is worth reading for what it signals about Apple's intent — but the credibility gap with the gaming community is real.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac: New App Store chief discusses Apple's gaming strategy, future of Apple Arcade, more
  • AppleInsider News: Apple still doesn't understand gamers in spite of iPhone being a gaming powerhouse

item.title: After $5.7B Verdict, Taction Wants a Cut of Future iPhone Sales Through 2035
item.description:
Taction Technology isn't stopping at its historic $5.7 billion patent infringement verdict against Apple. The company is now seeking additional damages and interest, plus ongoing royalties on future iPhone and Apple Watch sales stretching all the way to 2035. If granted, it would amount to a decade-long tax on Apple's two most important products — a reminder that the verdict's fallout is just beginning, with the final financial exposure still to be decided.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac: Following $5.7B verdict, Taction wants a cut of iPhone and Apple Watch sales through 2035

item.title: Two French Apple Stores Looted During Protests
item.description:
As protests in France escalated — with around 600,000 demonstrators in the streets — two Apple Stores were ransacked. Apple Sainte-Catherine in Bordeaux was hit first by groups of youths, followed a few hours later by the store in Lille. Apple wasn't alone as a target: Hermès and Louis Vuitton locations were also looted. There is no word yet on the extent of the damage to either store or when they might reopen.

Sources

  • AppleInsider News: Two Apple stores looted during French protests

item.title: iPhone Duo demand crushes supply as deliveries slip to January
item.description:
Apple's first foldable iPhone is a genuine smash, and a genuine supply-chain mess. The company said pre-order demand was "nothing short of extraordinary" after delivery dates slipped from the promised October 23 to late January within hours of orders opening. Apple Store employees have been told to expect no launch-day stock for walk-in buyers and to discourage them from showing up.

Bloomberg's Mark Gurman called the launch timing a "major mistake," arguing Apple knew severe manufacturing constraints were coming but shipped anyway to land the Duo in its fiscal first quarter. Apple, predictably, is playing the demand angle — but as John Gruber notes, only Apple knows how thin the inventory really was. Expect the backorder story to run for months.

Sources

  • Daring Fireball: Apple Issues Statement on Duo Demand Far Outstripping Supply
  • 512 Pixels: Duo Walk-In Purchases Discouraged
  • MacRumors: Mark Gurman: Apple Made 'Major Mistake' With iPhone Duo Pre-Orders

item.title: Gurman: HomeView units sat boxed in warehouses for nearly a year
item.description:
Mark Gurman's Power On column pulled back the curtain on Apple's smart home display: finished HomeView hardware has been sitting boxed in warehouses for most of the past year, waiting on software. The delays were all about the smarter Siri — Apple postponed the product repeatedly without a serviceable version of its new assistant.

The hardware also betrays its age: thick bezels, an A18 chip, and 8GB of memory make it clearly a product conceived years ago. Gruber couldn't resist pointing out that The Information wrongly reported this same device in January as an imminent launch with a "robotic swiveling base" — that version, it turns out, is still a year or more away.

Sources

  • Daring Fireball: Gurman on HomeView: 'Finished Units Have Been Sitting Boxed Up in Warehouses for the Better Part of a Year'

item.title: A 'HomeView Max' with a 360-degree robotic arm is rumored for 2027
item.description:
Apple's next act for HomeView is already in the rumor mill. According to Gurman, Apple plans a higher-end version — speculatively dubbed HomeView Max, Ultra, or 360 — with a larger 9-inch screen that can swivel a full 360 degrees on a motorized robotic arm, arriving in 2027 or 2028.

The logic is straightforward: the current $299 tabletop model's 7-inch fixed display only works well if you're sitting in front of it, a real limitation in a busy kitchen with people gathered around. Whether Apple can ship it on time given the years of Siri delays behind the original is the open question.

Sources

  • MacRumors: Apple Planning 'HomeView Max' With 9-Inch, 360-Degree Screen

item.title: EU energy label reveals iPhone Duo's 4,883 mAh battery
item.description:
Apple quietly uploaded an EU energy label confirming the iPhone Duo packs a 4,883 mAh battery — a 2,962 mAh cell plus a 1,921 mAh cell. That outstrips the eSIM-only iPhone 18 Pro's 4,288 mAh, though it's smaller than the 18 Pro Max's capacity.

Because the Duo is eSIM-only worldwide, this figure applies everywhere — no regional variant with a SIM tray and shrunken battery. For a foldable with two displays to feed, the number will fuel the real question of the Duo's first reviews: how that capacity translates into actual battery life.

Sources

  • MacRumors: Apple Reveals iPhone Duo's Battery Capacity
  • 9to5Mac: Here's how iPhone Duo's battery capacity compares to other iPhones

item.title: Apple expected to release new products on the next four Fridays
item.description:
Gurman says Apple's autumn blitz isn't over: new products are expected across the next four Fridays. After the iPhone Duo launch on October 23 and HomePod mini 2 on October 30, November 6 should bring OLED-display MacBook Pros — including Apple's first-ever touchscreen Mac — alongside M6 14-inch MacBook Pros and iMacs and an OLED iPad mini 8, announced as early as October 27 or 28.

The November 6 date gained support from a planned Apple Store retail reset that day. A touchscreen Mac is a remarkable reversal after more than a decade of Apple insisting touch didn't belong on the MacBook — expect it to be the headline product of the bunch.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac: Apple's first touchscreen MacBook could debut on November 6: Here's what to expect
  • AppleInsider News: Retail reset set for November 6 as OLED MacBook Pro looms

item.title: Verizon will charge $10/month for iPhone Handoff between two iPhones
item.description:
Verizon announced it will support iPhone Handoff — the feature that lets one phone number work seamlessly across two iPhones, swapping the active device at will — but at a price: $10/month for compatible iPhones running iOS 27.

The pitch is aimed squarely at Duo buyers who might pair the foldable with an iPhone 18 Pro. Carriers have been itching to monetize multi-device setups, and this is one of the clearest attempts yet. Whether customers accept a subscription on top of their plan for what is essentially number-sharing remains to be seen.

Sources

  • Daring Fireball: Verizon Is Going to Charge $10/Month for iPhone Handoff

item.title: Early discounts: Mac mini up to $149 off, Mac Studio $200 off at Amazon
item.description:
Amazon is cutting prices on Apple's newest Macs this weekend. The M6 Mac mini is up to $149 off — the 16GB/256GB model drops to $779.99 — while the M5 Max Mac Studio with 36GB of RAM and a 512GB SSD is $200 off at $2,299, the lowest price since its September 22 release.

The deals are notable mainly for their timing: discounting machines that are barely a month old suggests either healthy inventory or early holiday-season positioning. Either way, anyone who just bought at full price will be annoyed.

item.title: 2027 could bring a revamped iPhone lineup
item.description:
With the iPhone Duo backordered through January and the 18 Pro barely a month old, 9to5Mac is already looking ahead to 2027, when Apple is expected to shake up the iPhone lineup significantly.

Details are still thin, but the report frames next year's cycle as a genuine revamp rather than an iterative update. For anyone on the fence about the Duo or the 18 Pro, the takeaway is familiar: Apple always has something new a year out, but 2027 looks like it could be worth the wait.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac: Not upgrading to iPhone 18 Pro or Duo? Here's what's coming next year

item.title: OpenAI alleges an ex-employee stole unreleased device files and briefed Apple leadership
item.description:
The legal war between OpenAI and Apple just escalated sharply. According to Reuters, a new filing in US federal court in San Jose alleges that an OpenAI employee who defected to Apple sent more than 100 files about an unreleased OpenAI product to a personal account, then presented the unreleased product to senior Apple leadership months ago. OpenAI now claims Apple is making AI products of its own, pointing to this week's HomeView launch as evidence.

This is the kind of allegation that transforms a contract dispute into a potential trade-secrets case. If proven, it would mean one of Apple's marquee AI-adjacent products was informed by confidential material taken from a direct competitor, and it hands OpenAI enormous leverage. Expect discovery fights, a public relations brawl, and renewed scrutiny of how Apple builds its AI hardware strategy.

Sources

  • Daring Fireball: Whatever You Say Bounces Off Me and Sticks to You

item.title: Apple tells retail staff to warn iPhone Duo shoppers away from launch-day walk-ins
item.description:
If you were hoping to stroll into an Apple Store on Friday, October 23 and walk out with an iPhone Duo, Apple's own staff are being told to talk you out of it. MacRumors reports that retail employees have been instructed to warn customers without pre-orders that there will likely be no iPhone Duo stock for walk-in purchases on launch day, and Apple's online store is directing shoppers to check back Saturday, October 24 for pickup availability.

The memo reads as both a demand signal and a supply warning: the Duo, Apple's first foldable iPhone, is seeing pre-order demand strong enough to push delivery estimates back by months. For prospective buyers the takeaway is simple — pre-order is the only reliable path, and launch-day store visits will likely end in disappointment.

Sources

  • MacRumors: Apple Retail Staff Told to Warn Against iPhone Duo Walk-In Purchases
  • 9to5Mac: iPhone Duo walk-in purchases might be challenging at launch, per report

item.title: Apple hires former Meta litigation chief Scott Tucker to run global legal battles
item.description:
Apple is bolstering its legal bench. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports that Apple has hired Scott Tucker, the former head of litigation at Meta (and previously a senior legal figure at Morgan Stanley), to become vice president of global litigation and financial services — a new role overseeing commercial lawsuits, patent disputes, and legal matters tied to Apple's financial products. Tucker reunites with general counsel Jennifer Newstead, who herself joined Apple from Meta in March.

The hire lands amid a year of leadership reshuffling under new CEO John Ternus, and it arrives just as Apple's legal exposure is swelling — from the escalating OpenAI trade-secrets fight to the usual thicket of patent and antitrust battles. Bringing in a seasoned Big Tech litigator who has sat on the other side of some of those fights looks like deliberate preparation for a litigious few years.

Sources

  • MacRumors: Apple Hires Former Meta Lawyer to Oversee Global Litigation
  • AppleInsider News: Apple nabs Meta VP for global litigation chief role

item.title: Apple cracks down on bait-and-switch AI "nudify" apps
item.description:
Apple has updated the App Review Guidelines in a targeted crackdown on apps that generate non-consensual adult imagery. The problem isn't just the apps themselves, which were already prohibited — it's that developers have been using bait-and-switch tactics to slip them past review, submitting innocuous-looking apps that reveal their true "nudify" functionality after approval.

The update tightens how review treats deceptive submissions and reinforces that this entire category is banned. It matters because AI image-generation tools have made this abuse far easier to build and harder to detect, and the App Store's gatekeeping is Apple's main defense for users who can't vet code themselves. Expect similar whack-a-mole updates as developers keep probing the boundaries.

Sources

  • AppleInsider News: AI nudify apps targeted in App Review Guidelines update

item.title: Rosetta is going away in macOS 27 — IT fleets should start planning now
item.description:
Installing macOS 27, codenamed Golden Gate, will automatically remove Rosetta — the translation layer that has let Intel apps run on Apple silicon Macs for six years. For IT administrators, that means any lingering x86-only software in the fleet will simply stop working, and the time to audit and replace it is now rather than at upgrade time.

Rosetta's long goodbye was always on the roadmap, but making removal automatic at install is a hard cutover that will catch organizations with forgotten legacy tools off guard. Fleet managers should be inventorying Intel-only apps, pushing vendors for native Apple silicon builds, and staging test upgrades before the rollout. The transition era is ending; the clock is officially running.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac: Apple @ Work: How I'm preparing my fleet for Rosetta's removal in macOS 27

item.title: Gruber asks the awkward question about HomeView: why do you need it?
item.description:
After a week of HomeView coverage, John Gruber lands the critique Apple hasn't answered: why does this product need to exist? Apple's launch video doesn't say, and even imagining a HomeView set up in your home, he argues, it's unclear when you'd reach for it instead of your phone — or just talk to a screenless HomePod.

The piece cuts at the core risk of the category. Smart displays have been tried and abandoned by nearly everyone else, and Apple's differentiator — deep HomeKit integration and privacy — may not be enough if the device solves no real problem. If the broader verdict lands where Gruber's does, HomeView could become the new AirPods-scale bet that misfires. Either way, the next few months of reviews and sales will tell.

Sources

  • Daring Fireball: HomeView Thoughts and Observations

item.title: iPhone Duo pre-orders open, sell out into 2027 within minutes
item.description:
Apple's first foldable iPhone went up for pre-order Friday morning at 5 a.m. Pacific in more than 70 countries, and demand immediately overwhelmed supply. Within minutes, U.S. delivery estimates slipped from launch-day October 23 into November; by 5:30 a.m. every configuration was quoting January 25, and Apple is no longer taking orders for 2026 delivery. Apple called demand "nothing short of extraordinary" in a statement to the Financial Times.

The $1,999 foldable (5.4 inches closed, 7.6 inches open) is already commanding premiums on the secondary market: one eBay listing for a Night Sky 2TB unit — $3,199 from Apple — sold for $5,000, an $1,800 markup. Carriers are chasing demand too, with AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon offering up to $1,200 in bill credits via trade-ins, and up to $800 just for switching to AT&T. Whether the frenzy reflects genuine demand or constrained supply is unknowable, but scalpers don't usually pay an $1,800 premium on a dud.

item.title: Verizon will charge $10/month for iPhone Handoff
item.description:
Apple's new iPhone Handoff feature in iOS 27 — which lets one phone number be shared across two separate iPhones — now has a price tag from Verizon: $10 per month, confirmed as part of the carrier's iPhone Duo announcement. Verizon will support Handoff on the iPhone Duo and the iPhone 18 Pro models, pitching the ability to use one number seamlessly across the pocketable foldable and a second iPhone.

Verizon is the third carrier to name its price, following T-Mobile and Deutsche Telekom. The feature's pitch is obvious alongside the Duo — carry the foldable on the go and keep your number on it too — but carriers clearly see it as subscription revenue rather than a free convenience. No carrier has broken ranks yet, so $10/month is shaping up as the going rate for one number on two iPhones.

item.title: Apple cracks down on AI nudify apps and bait-and-switch apps in App Review Guidelines
item.description:
Apple strengthened its App Review Guidelines today with new rules targeting AI-generated nonconsensual intimate imagery and "bait-and-switch" apps. Sexually explicit content was already banned, but the updated 1.2 rule now requires developers to proactively prevent and remove AI-generated deepfakes from their platforms, and Apple warns apps with offending content can be removed from the App Store. The rule explicitly covers AI content-creation apps — a shot that could reach apps like xAI's Grok, whose chatbot users have complained about being used to generate nude and sexualized deepfakes.

Apple also reminded developers that apps containing hidden or undocumented features are prohibited, including apps that misrepresent themselves during review. Apps hosting user-generated content must filter objectionable material, give users reporting tools, and allow blocking abusive accounts. It's a meaningful tightening that puts platforms like Grok squarely in the blast radius.

item.title: Epic, PayPal warn DOJ a weak Apple antitrust settlement solves nothing
item.description:
The Information reports that PayPal and Epic Games are among the developers worried the Department of Justice's potential antitrust settlement with Apple will be toothless. More than two years after the DOJ sued Apple in a sweeping antitrust case, officials have reportedly signaled they favor a negotiated resolution and have asked developers to propose improvements to how the iPhone interoperates with other companies' products.

Epic fears the DOJ is about to let Apple off with a deal that does nothing to deter future App Store behavior, and PayPal is aligned. The dynamic is familiar: Apple claims reform while preserving control over the iPhone's key chokepoints. The DOJ hasn't settled — but the developers who would be most affected are already signaling that whatever's on the table isn't enough.

item.title: Apple hires longtime Meta executive to lead global litigation
item.description:
Bloomberg reports that Apple has poached Scott Tucker, who spent nearly six years as Meta's vice president and deputy general counsel for global litigation, to lead its own global litigation efforts. The hire lands at a moment when Apple's legal plate is full: the DOJ antitrust case heading toward a possible settlement, the ongoing saga with Epic over App Store rules, and regulatory fights worldwide.

Bringing in a veteran of Meta's legal wars suggests Apple is staffing up for a long, grinding phase of litigation rather than expecting quick resolutions. Tucker knows what it looks like from the other side of the industry's biggest courtroom battles. It matters because Apple's legal strategy increasingly is its business strategy — whether the DOJ settlement holds, whether App Store rules survive, all of it will be decided by lawyers like this one.

item.title: HomeView pre-order discounts appear as wait times push into December
item.description:
Pre-orders are live on Apple's newest devices — the $299 HomeView smart home hub and the new $299 Apple TV 4K — and Amazon has already issued the first-ever discounts on both: a modest $9 off the Apple TV 4K to $289.99, plus early HomeView pre-order discounts, along with launch-day delivery in some cases.

item.title: Elevation Lab pulls AirTag Silencer after admitting it aids stalking
item.description:
Accessory maker Elevation Lab has withdrawn its AirTag Silencer and issued an apology after acknowledging the tool could help people track victims without their knowledge. The product was a jig that let an AirTag owner remove the battery, slot the AirTag in, and drive a pin into the tracker's speaker with a hammer — permanently disabling the audible alert designed to warn people they're being tracked, while leaving every other component intact.

It's a welcome reversal. AirTags have been misused for stalking since launch, and Apple's entire mitigation strategy — speaker chirps and separation alerts — depends on the speaker working. A mainstream product that turned silencing into a ten-minute hammer project crossed a clear line. Elevation Lab gets credit for admitting it and killing the product rather than selling through the inventory.

item.title: GF Securities: Apple the only major phone maker growing shipments in 2026
item.description:
GF Securities analysts Jeff Pu and Henry Huang project Apple will be the only major smartphone manufacturer to grow shipments in 2026, even as the global market is expected to shrink by more than 14% — a striking divergence that underscores how premium demand has held up while the broader market contracts.

The note also flags challenges ahead for the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo, presumably around supply and the premium pricing gauntlet ($1,999 for the foldable). It frames Apple's 2026 position: winning a shrinking market is good, but it means the company is increasingly dependent on high-end buyers and launch-day blockbusters like the Duo sellout to keep the growth story alive.

item.title: iPhone Duo pre-orders open Friday, and repairs won't be cheap
item.description:

Meanwhile CEO John Ternus landed on the cover of TIME's Best Inventions of 2026, calling early foldables 'kind of cheap and crappy' and revealing he and five engineers patented foldable concepts back in 2011. Apple execs also pushed back on claims it's 'just using a Samsung display,' describing Samsung as a key supplier of a display Apple designed.

item.title: Meta and Apple team up to run a 800B-parameter AI model on Mac Studio
item.description:
Meta released Muse Spark Open, which it calls the 'most capable U.S. open-weight model to date': a multimodal large language model with over 800 billion parameters (around 40 billion active per token via mixture-of-experts), built for coding, software engineering, and multi-step tasks.

The surprise is the hardware story. Meta worked directly with Apple to optimize the model for the Mac, and it can run locally on a desktop setup of two 512GB M5 Ultra Mac Studios (or four 256GB machines) using Apple's MLX framework — no cloud required. Mark Zuckerberg publicly thanked John Ternus for the collaboration, and Ternus replied that 'Mac Studio keeps pushing the boundaries of on-device AI.' For developers who want frontier-class open models without a data center, this is a milestone.

item.title: Apple pledged $25 million to Trump's White House ballroom
item.description:
The Washington Post obtained a donor list showing Apple pledged $25 million toward President Trump's White House ballroom project, making it one of the largest donors alongside Nvidia ($25 million) and the Adelson family. The list totals $333 million in private donations from companies including Microsoft, Comcast, Amazon, Cisco, Meta, T-Mobile, HP, Palantir, Salesforce, and Micron — plus Google, whose contribution came from a lawsuit settlement.

The story's bite is who's on the list and why it was secret: the Post notes previously undisclosed contributors who have benefited from regulatory decisions, government contracts, and in one case a pardon for a family member. The White House has never publicly disclosed the donation amounts, though political giving of this kind typically requires disclosure. The White House declined to comment on individual donors.

item.title: OpenAI vows not to use Apple's trade secrets as injunction looms
item.description:
Apple's July 2026 lawsuit against OpenAI over alleged trade secret theft — files allegedly taken by ex-Apple employees who joined OpenAI — took a sharp turn: after the judge said he was 'highly likely' to grant Apple's injunction, OpenAI volunteered not to use any proprietary Apple information while the case continues, effectively conceding the substance without formally admitting it. Apple has also issued its official response to OpenAI's allegations.

Separately, in a TIME interview, marketing chief Greg Joswiak drew a bright line between Apple Intelligence and the frontier-model world: Apple builds AI for 'everyday people,' not the 'lunatic fringe' of die-hard AI believers in Silicon Valley. He also said Apple doesn't feel threatened by OpenAI's hardware ambitions. It's the clearest statement yet of Apple's AI positioning: modest, personalized, privacy-preserving — and pointedly not chasing the hype cycle.

item.title: Withings puts Apple Health syncing behind a $100/year paywall for new users
item.description:
Withings, maker of smart scales that measure 60+ biomarkers, has gated one of its most basic features: anyone who created a Withings account on or after October 13, 2026 must pay for Withings+ ($99.50/year in the U.S.) to auto-sync data to third-party apps including Apple Health. Existing accounts are grandfathered in.

The change is striking because Apple Health integration was long advertised as a core feature of Withings products, and free syncing to Apple's Health app is effectively table stakes for health hardware in the Apple ecosystem. The company is betting new buyers won't balk at a subscription costing nearly as much as some of its scales. Expect this to become a cautionary example in 'everything is a subscription' discourse — and a reason to buy health gear from brands that don't ransom your own data back to you.

item.title: Apple closes above $5 trillion for the first time
item.description:
Apple became only the second company ever to close a trading day with a market capitalization above $5 trillion, following Nvidia's milestone last October. The stock finished Wednesday at $342.96, for a valuation of $5.005 trillion. Apple had crossed the $5 trillion line intraday six times before, but this is the first time it held into the close.

The milestone arrives just over a month after John Ternus succeeded Tim Cook as CEO and two days before pre-orders open for the iPhone Duo, Apple's first foldable. Investors appear to be betting that strong iPhone 18 Pro demand and the Duo launch will carry the stock higher, even as Apple fights a bruising trade-secrets battle with OpenAI and races to bring Apple Intelligence to China.

item.title: Apple and OpenAI trade fresh accusations in escalating trade-secrets fight

Apple told Reuters it has found no evidence to support the claims.

The tit-for-tat filings mark a sharp escalation. OpenAI even implied Apple's new HomeView may have been influenced by the alleged theft. Expect the forensic investigation at the heart of the case to keep both companies' hardware plans under a microscope for months.

item.title: Apple Intelligence finally heads to China in December — without Siri AI
item.description:
After two years of regulatory wrangling, Apple will bring Apple Intelligence to China in iOS 27.3, expected this December, according to Bloomberg. The launch will cover basic features like photo editing, but Siri AI, Image Playground, and the new Genmoji won't make the cut, and text-generation tools will be limited.

China's strict AI rules required Apple to route its features through local models; the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology recently granted network access permits for Alibaba's Qwen and Tongyi Wanxiang models on the iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro, and earlier iPhones. It's a long-overdue unlock of AI features in one of Apple's most important markets — though the trimmed-down version means Chinese users wait longer still for the full Siri AI experience.

At equivalent storage the Duo costs $800 more than the iPhone 18 Pro while asking buyers to accept roughly 40 compromises — from camera capabilities to everyday usability — in exchange for the folding 7.6-inch inner display. With a $1,999 starting price, AppleCare+ looks close to mandatory, exactly as Apple intends.

item.title: Apple clears up the Siri AI rollout confusion — original HomePod mini misses out
item.description:
A day after its home-device launch blitz, Apple drew the Siri AI support lines. The original HomePod mini (S5 chip) will not get Siri AI, Apple confirmed, correcting a CNET report that had claimed otherwise. Siri AI ships at launch on November 13 with HomeView and the 4th-gen Apple TV 4K; the 2nd- and 3rd-gen Apple TV 4K get it in tvOS 27.2; and the HomePod mini 2 — shipping October 30 with an S10 chip — won't get Siri AI until a future software update. Two clues on Apple's website suggest the full-size HomePod 2 may eventually join the club, though Apple hasn't confirmed it.

The staggered rollout underscores how deeply the new Siri depends on recent silicon: Siri AI requests involving personal context also require an Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone or iPad. If you're counting on smarter Siri at home, the fine print matters more than the keynote.

item.title: HomeView fallout: FCC filing reveals 2024 testing, $279 repair fee, CarPlay-based app story
item.description:
New details keep surfacing about Apple's $299 HomeView, launching November 13. An FCC filing shows the device was undergoing regulatory testing in October 2024 running what would now be called HomeView software version 18 — the clearest evidence yet that its two-year delay was caused by the Siri AI holdup, resolved only with Siri AI's launch this September.

Apple's specs page lists 15 built-in apps (Home, FaceTime, Music, Intercom, and more) and confirms there's no App Store: third-party support comes via CarPlay-enabled audio and video apps from a paired iPhone — Spotify, YouTube, Netflix, and others can appear if they opt in, plus third-party iPhone widgets work. AppleInsider warns the CarPlay entitlement process, designed for cars, could be a bottleneck for home developers. And the fine print stings: Apple charges a flat $279 to repair a $299 HomeView without AppleCare — 93% of the price of a new one.
